Design v. Evolution and the Role Played by the Mystery of Randomness

Forming what is perhaps Dembski's most pivotal argument (perhaps also the most philosophically interesting aspect of his case) is the proposition that, given the possibility for intelligent design in nature being a true fact, the possibility for detecting it is methodologically eliminated by the sciences. That method characterizes the underlying structure of nature's processes as describable only via the backdrop of brute chance, combined with the antagonism against chance of the purely contingent outcomes of deterministic laws of nature. In effect, by accepting this a priori explanatory mode, we preclude ourselves from ever detecting intelligent design, even given the case where it is possible.

Therefore, it becomes necessary to ask the question as to whether there could be a formalizable technique and combined set of criteria for truthfully picking out the signature of intelligent design. More straightforwardly, if intelligent design is possible, it's worth questioning how we'd even recognize it if we were looking at it.

I'm interested to take up a rather implicit part of the logic behind Dembski's CSI, and make a simple case that this logic is self-defeating (at least insofar as it supports the specificity supposedly built into CSI's filter for explanation).

In Dembski's chapter from the book Debating Design: From Darwin to DNA (Cambridge Press, 2004), he describes a conference which took place in 1988 at Ohio State University, where many prominent logicians and statisticians convened to discuss randomness. In the end, the goal of the meeting was to publish something of a definitive description of randomness itself. Providing several quotations from its participants, Dembski tells us that, despite reaching agreement about several things that randomness was not, the meeting represented a complete failure to give a positive account for what randomness actually was. They discovered that every theory from the complexity or information-theoretic standpoint shared the feature of defining randomness only as a negation of non-randomness, i.e. only when we could specify something that was non-random could we even produce the necessary conditions for saying how it could be random. One crucial subject of this meeting was random number generators. Dembski tells us:

As I reflected on this asymmetry between randomness and nonrandomness, it became clear that randomness was not an intrinsic property of objects. Instead, randomness was a provisional designation for describing an absence of perceive pattern, until such time as a pattern was perceived, at which time the object in question would no longer be considered random. In the case of random number generators, for instance, the statistical tests relative to which their adequacy was assessed constituted a set of patterns. So long as the random number generator passed all these tests, it was considered random. But as soon as a statistical test was discovered that the random number generator no longer passed, it was no longer good and its output was considered nonrandom. George Marsaglia, a leading light in random number generation who spoke at the 1988 randomness conference, made this point beautifully, detailing one failed random number generator after another.

The problem with this might not at first be so obvious. You might say, "Well that is just fine. Randomness is a condition defined by the absence of non-randomness. The problem arises insofar as science posits randomness as physically primitive. The universe is thought, with various subtleties of mechanism, to have arisen by a process of chance. Whether this is the random possibility for a singularity, or a white hole or quantum fluctuation is not important. The cosmologies which imagine our universe as having tunneled from a nearby or pre-existing universe hardly defeat the problem, rather, they only push it back by one more universe. If randomness is contingent on non-randomness, how could randomness be antecedent to pattern in the universe? Viewed this way, I believe it makes a fairly strong and uniquely-framed cosmological sort of argument.

Randomness doesn't appear to be 'given'. On the contrary, it is what must be accounted for in the universe that we actually find. It is not even evident what constitutes intelligence itself is, by nature, even capable of creating or registering randomness.

Dembski summarizes:

If randomness just means violating every possible pattern from a set of known patterns, then anything can be random relative to a suitable set of patterns (each one of which is violated).

This fully relativizes randomness. Dembski goes on to point out that some non-randomness is still taken to be more random than others. This involves a case about statistical significance, which I won't get into here. I'd instead like to just consider the notion of an actually non-random universe. While this is taken by some, including Dembski, to be case positive for CSI, I'd like to suggest that it actually deflates CSI.

My question is a simple one. What is the metaphysical possibility for or against a universe that is patterned? If it is just the case that we happen to be in a universe which was patterned, why should it strike us as strange or unexpected that what we find are just various degrees of hierarchical "pattern-ness"?

It seems to me that the ID community would like to argue, first by accepting the scientific community's premise that the universe was inherently random, while also arguing that randomness is so difficult for mankind (intelligence) to achieve that it's likely an impossibility except with strict boundary conditions relative to to the pattern-detecting capacities of any observer.

Yet it is my intuition that an abiding universe, that is one persisting across time is exactly what we should expect, given that non-randomness is the presence of pattern. To understand this requires the realization that pattern itself consists in symmetry, and fundamentally, symmetry itself is redundancy to varying degrees which determine the level of symmetry.

I'd like to say that we could construe existence itself as a form of redundancy, simply that form of redundancy that respects time instead of simultaneous tokens (in other words: every moment in time becomes a token against which every other token is a redundancy). If not for this basic fact of universal nature, there'd not be a universe to appreciate. If existence is redundancy across time, then a patterned universe is tautological. Pattern is necessary for an intelligible existence.

Given that the human organism evolved contingently in the patterned universe, randomness is neither possible to incorporate into cognitive processes (except by very non-random means), so neither can it be present as such in the outcomes of thought. We are simply unable to deal with randomness. For example, given a randomly generated string of numbers of any length, to say the string is random only begs the question. It is only left for an intelligence of sufficient magnitude which is capable of computing across this number of values to find that it has a pattern. For any sequence, there always exists a possible digit, which added to the terminus of the string, might instantiate a pattern.

Randomness just becomes the property by which a finite intelligence specifies the absence of a pattern. I'd argue that in the case of DNA, we are dealing with just such a pattern, but this is precisely why the DNA encodes for downstream patterns that do communicate meaningfully to the organisms bearing the genome. It communicates an unintelligible pattern, through step-wise physiological patterns that build the phenotype, a form of symmetry (say, in facial structure) by which we infer causally, the necessary information existed within the sequential genetic information.

The overarching point is that the universe just is patterned. If pattern can build on top of pattern, where one transmits it's symmetry to the next level of structure, then in such a universe CSI never gets off of the ground. What does happen is that CSI reduces to a cosmological argument. Once we have a patterned universe, explaining more contingent pattern is not difficult especially with the universal symmetry-producing effects of thermodynamic laws (making information and entropy symmetrical for the whole). Rather, the problem is still one of how a pattern might come from a pattern-less substrate, or nothing at all. I believe that CSI errors because of its specificity, but retains its logic if it is generalized to a cosmological scope.

A patterned universe causes us a great difficulty to explain given a randomized starting point (after all, when it is not evident that randomness can exist without non-randomness). DNA does not if the very first instances of existence in the universe come to exist on the basis of inherent pattern and redundancy.

This is reminiscent of the weak anthropic principle. If a patterned universe (alternatively, a fine-tuned universe) is necessary for life to exist at all, then given the a posteriori fact that life exists, we should not be surprised to find the universe patterned. Of course it is the a priori probability that is of concern, which is why naturalists citing the WAP as a solution to fine-tuning arguments invariably end up insisting on the existence of a multiverse.

I won't deny that this cosmological issue is related to the CSI argument. Given our universe is patterned (it is evidently fine-tuned for life), then we should be no more surprised to find patterns / CSI than life itself, since a universe fine-tuned for life is also a universe fine-tuned for CSI. This is also where the "strong" category of the strong anthropic principle (rather than the weak) becomes relevant: given the nature of this universe, it could be said that life emerging (and thus CSI) was in fact compelled.

But we have to recall what the theorem accomplishes. Dembski's theorem does not draw a distinction between randomness and design; it draws a distinction between all natural processes and design (as modes of causality). Put another way, it gauges the grounds at which is is no longer reasonable to suppose that non-intentional processes were responsible for an event. Naturalists will obviously insist that even intentional processes are natural processes; this doesn't matter. The theorem is simply concerned with distinguishing between intentional and non-intentional processes, since this is a distinction to which even naturalists will admit. The theorem thus provides, again, objective means of establishing when it is no longer tenable to suppose an event was unintentional. This becomes meaningful when we apply the theorem to events that precede all known naturalistic intentional processes. Obviously if the existence of DNA is an event with abundant CSI, then it follows that DNA was an intended event (for the moment taking this to possibly include naturalistic processes that are intentional). If we then find that there are no naturalistic processes that we could describe as intentional prior to the existence of DNA, then we are forced to acknowledge the objectively indicated existence of a nonnatural or supernatural intentional process.

So I don't think drawing a distinction between patterned and non-patterned is sufficient. Recall that the component, T, is a conceptual component that specifies the event E. It is not just that stars are spherical and thus symmetrical, or that dividing 1 by 9 yields a repeating and non-terminating decimal, that constitutes CSI. It is that a circle can be drawn on a wall and arrows shot at it specifically, or letters typed on paper specifically to communicate a story...or that molecules can be arranged into a code specifically to allow for animated life forms that constitutes CSI.

I said above that a universe that compels life, a la the strong anthropic principle, likewise compels CSI. I did not admit that such a universe compels life (or CSI) without it first being specifically set up to do so. In the same way that I, a man, can make use of natural means in addition to the vertical means of my intellect, to bring about a painting, or a novel, or a functioning computer program, so too can God create natural processes and laws and initial conditions such that, not only are the universal constants arranged to allow for life to form, but the initial conditions are also arranged such that, at t = 10 billion years, a planet will form within a certain distance of a star of a certain size and radiance, and that, at t = 11 billion years, the exact naturalistic processes that need to occur, in the precise quantities and timings, will take place such that organic molecules and proteins forms, and then at t = 11.5 billion years, these molecules will then be formed into a specific code in order to allow for the eventual appearance of creatures capable of receiving, vertically, a rational soul. What Dembski's theorem provides is the ability to say on objective grounds, that for these processes to have brought about the CSI found within DNA, even given a patterned universe, then these processes must have been intentional. For this to have occurred without intentionality is so momentously improbable, on rigorous and objectively demonstrable grounds, that it simply cannot be admitted.

Please understand that Dembski's theorem does not prove that intermittent miracles throughout the course of history were necessary to allow for the emergence of DNA. Such a "divine adjustment" theory of creation is both uncompelling and insulting to God's glory. The theorem simply states that natural processes that do enable change in this universe, from the initial conditions to the laws to the very universal constants themselves, must have been intended - which is to say, designed - for the sake of this complex specified result. Attempts to explain these complex specified effects without invoking intentionality are excluded as too improbable on rigorous mathematical grounds.

That is the proof.
